fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The sayings of the high one", "body": "Chance Garton frames the Havamal, the sayings of the high one, as poetry that carries the words of Odin and the everyday morality of the Old Norse. Benjamin Balderson and Rachel Maiden have spent eight episodes of Odin's Alchemy on its hundred and sixty stanzas, reading several translations side by side because the wording changes everything. Balderson compares confident translation to digging up an unknown creature and inventing the sound it made, and says small shifts can flip a passage the way a nature documentary frames the same hunt as a starving mother or as doomed prey."}, {"title": "Hospitality was survival, not manners", "body": "The guest rights and host rights that dominate the poem were not etiquette but life and death. Balderson describes five feet of snow at his own place and says that if somebody showed up at his door and he refused them, they could die. Chance Garton adds that a natural law society needs very few rules, mostly a short list of things you should not do, which leaves room for hospitality, and that a high trust society is a productive and healthy one. Rachel Maiden notes how far modern Viking culture has drifted from that."}, {"title": "Gullveig and the sickness of hoarding", "body": "Chance Garton reads a stanza about saving for the loathed what was meant for the loved, and hears a warning against hoarding against disaster instead of sharing with the people you love. Balderson answers with Gullveig, the real villain of heathen cosmology, who embodies a hoard valued above a man, and with the modern case of the state clawing back an estate after Medicaid care. Rachel Maiden describes possessions split in thirds at death, one part for the funeral, one for family, and one utterly destroyed, then asks what a billionaire living that way would leave behind."}, {"title": "Odin, the mead of poetry and the ferryman", "body": "Because Odin is said to live on wine alone and to have stolen the mead of poetry, Chance Garton connects him to Bacchus, to Dionysus and to Indra stealing ambrosia. He traces a pun in the poem between forgetfulness and a river mouth, and links the heron of the drinking stanzas to Charon, the ferryman on the river of forgetting. Balderson, a mead maker, insists not every drink was meant to intoxicate, separating a mead of knowledge from party drinking, and recalls Rome winning battles by feeding Germans stronger wine. Rachel Maiden reads Odin's ravens, thought and memory, as drinking to remember."}, {"title": "You are your own judge", "body": "Balderson says heathens face no external judge at death. He is the judge, which he compares to the Egyptian heart weighed against a feather, and it makes him live by a strict moral code because he will eat himself up over failing it. Rachel Maiden defines heathen simply as a country person, and notes that Crestos in Greek meant good, so a person could be a heathen and a Crestian at once. Chance Garton argues that if the world is as within so without, then morality is built into reality itself, an energy that constricts or flows."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Tonight we're joined by Odin's favorite wizard, Benjamin Balderson, and the poetic paganist Rachel Maiden, for an examination of customs and philosophy selected from the Hávamál, and other works of the Poetic Eddas. These two have a great knowledge of Norse Mythology and the morality that it espouses, along with a strong grasp upon the wisdom of the runes, as they've been teaching on the Odin's Alchemy podcast.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: The Plus+ Extension begins with discussion on the value of difference between regional deities, and by the end we find ourselves in a hilarious set of Odin's observations about the differences between men and women. This is a truly unique second hour, worth the price of admission.
